lead: This unit finds the one point through which a shape's weight can be taken to act, and the numbers that describe how the shape's area or mass is spread about an axis. After it you can locate the centroid of a line, an area or a volume, compute second moments and products of inertia about any axis, find the principal axes, and work out the mass moment of inertia of plates and common solids.
about: The unit turns geometry into numbers a designer can use. Chapter 4.1 defines centre of gravity and centroid and gives the symmetry shortcuts for lines and areas. Chapter 4.2 does the same job by integration and by composite tables, including volumes. Chapter 4.3 feeds those centroids into the theorems of Pappus-Guldinus to get surface areas and volumes of revolution. Chapter 4.4 introduces the second moment of area with the standard results, and 4.5 moves it to any parallel axis and to the polar axis. Chapter 4.6 adds the polar moment and the radius of gyration. Chapter 4.7 adds the product of inertia and finds the principal axes. Chapter 4.8 repeats the whole idea with mass, for plates and solids.

chapters.idea: The weight of a body acts through a single point, and for a thin line or a flat area that point is the average of the positions of all its elements, weighted by length or by area.
chapters.depth: Define centre of gravity, centre of mass and centroid, and say clearly that the centroid is a purely geometric point. Introduce the first moment of area Q = A x̄ and the first moment of length, with units mm³ and mm². Give the symmetry rules: if the figure has an axis of symmetry the centroid lies on it, and if it has two, the centroid is at their intersection. Standard results to know by heart: straight line at its midpoint, semicircular arc at 2r/π from the centre on the axis of symmetry, quarter arc at 2r/π from each radius, triangle at one third of the height from the base. Some syllabi call the same point the centre of area. Use lengths in mm and radii in mm throughout.

nodes.label: Sum moments about y-axis
nodes.note: γ A x̄ = Σ γ x dA

figure.aria: A flat area is split into small elements whose weights are summed, giving the centroid rule x̄ equals the sum of x dA divided by A.

chapters.example: A uniform wire is bent into an L: a 300 mm length lying along the x-axis from (0, 0) to (300, 0), and a 400 mm length standing vertically from (300, 0) to (300, 400). Find the centroid of the wire. Segment 1: L₁ = 300 mm, centroid (150, 0). Segment 2: L₂ = 400 mm, centroid (300, 200). Total length L = 700 mm. x̄ = (300 × 150 + 400 × 300) / 700 = 165000 / 700 = 235.7 mm. ȳ = (300 × 0 + 400 × 200) / 700 = 80000 / 700 = 114.3 mm. The centroid lies outside the wire itself, which is normal.
chapters.trap: Weighting by the wrong quantity — length for a wire, area for a plate, volume for a solid — and forgetting that a hole carries a negative area or negative volume in the sum.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for the idea of a force as a vector with a line of action; first-year integration for the element dA.
chapters.leave: Full integration and composite tables go to 4.2; volume centroids go to 4.2; the shift to other axes goes to 4.5.

chapters.idea: When a shape is not a standard figure, the weighted average becomes an integral; when it is built from standard figures, the same average becomes a table.
chapters.depth: Centroid of an area by single and double integration, choosing vertical strips (element dA = y dx, centroid at y/2) or horizontal strips, whichever needs one integral. Centroid of a line by integration, ds = √(dx² + dy²). Centroid of a volume by integration and by composite volumes using V x̄ = Σ V x̄, with volumes in mm³. Composite area and composite line tables: a sketch, a column of areas, a column of x̄, a column of A x̄, and holes entered as negative rows. Keep the boundary curves to straight lines, circles and simple parabolas. Report answers to three significant figures.

figure.title: T-section table, A in mm², Aȳ in 10³ mm³
figure.aria: A composite table for a T-section lists the web and the flange with their areas, centroid heights and area times centroid, and the total row gives the answer 67.8 mm.

chapters.example: Find the centroid of a T-section made of a web 20 mm wide and 80 mm tall, with a flange 100 mm wide and 20 mm thick on top. Take y from the bottom of the web. Web: A = 1600 mm², ȳ = 40 mm, Aȳ = 64000 mm³. Flange: A = 2000 mm², ȳ = 80 + 10 = 90 mm, Aȳ = 180000 mm³. Total A = 3600 mm², Σ Aȳ = 244000 mm³. ȳ = 244000 / 3600 = 67.8 mm above the base. The section is symmetric about the vertical centre line, so x̄ = 50 mm.
chapters.trap: Measuring x̄ and ȳ from different reference lines for different rows of the table, or taking the centroid height of a rectangle as its full height instead of half of it.
chapters.prereq: 4.1 for the centroid definition and the first moment of area; first-year integration of polynomials.
chapters.leave: Using these centroids to get surface areas and volumes goes to 4.3; shifting second moments to another axis goes to 4.5.

chapters.idea: Sweeping a plane curve about an external axis in its plane sweeps out a surface whose area is the curve length times the distance travelled by its centroid, and sweeping a plane area the same way gives a volume in the same form.
chapters.depth: State both theorems with formulas: surface area S = 2π x̄ L, where L is the curve length in mm and x̄ is the distance of the curve centroid from the axis in mm, and volume V = 2π x̄ A, where A is the plane area in mm² and x̄ the distance of the area centroid from the axis. State the condition: the axis must lie in the plane and must not cut the curve or the area. Work the theorems in both directions: find a surface or a volume from a known centroid, and find a centroid from tabulated surface area or volume. Applications: torus, hemispherical shell, cone surface, a belt over a pulley rim, a solid of revolution turned on a lathe.

figure.title: Two theorems, one idea
figure.aria: A curve of length L swept about an axis gives surface area 2π x̄ L, and a plane area A swept about the same axis gives volume 2π x̄ A.

chapters.example: A ring of circular cross-section is made by revolving a circle of radius 50 mm whose centre is 200 mm from the axis. Find the surface area and the volume. Curve: the circle perimeter L = 2π × 50 = 314.16 mm, centroid 200 mm from the axis. Surface area S = 2π × 200 × 314.16 = 394784 mm², about 0.395 m². Area: A = π × 50² = 7853.98 mm², centroid 200 mm from the axis. Volume V = 2π × 200 × 7853.98 = 9869604 mm³, about 9.87 × 10⁶ mm³.
chapters.trap: Using the distance from the axis to the nearest edge instead of to the centroid, and applying the theorems when the axis cuts the area, which double counts part of the sweep.
chapters.prereq: 4.1 and 4.2 for the centroid of a curve and of an area.
chapters.leave: Second moments of the swept surface or solid belong to 4.4 and 4.8.

chapters.idea: The second moment of area adds up each element of area multiplied by the square of its distance from the axis, so it measures how far the area is spread out and it decides how stiff a beam is in bending.
chapters.depth: Define I = ∫ y² dA about the x-axis, with y in mm and I in mm⁴. Explain why the name moment of inertia of an area is misleading: there is no mass and no rotation, only a distance-weighted sum of area. Derive I for a rectangle by a strip: b h³/12 about the centroidal axis, b h³/3 about the base. Quote and use: triangle b h³/36 about its centroidal axis, circle πd⁴/64 about a diameter, hollow circle π(D⁴ − d⁴)/64. Show that doubling the depth multiplies I by eight while doubling the width only doubles it. Ties to bending in later courses: a beam's stiffness comes from I, not from A.

figure.aria: A plot shows the second moment of area of a rectangle rising as the cube of the depth and far outrunning a straight-line comparison.

chapters.example: A timber beam has a rectangular section 120 mm wide and 200 mm deep. Find the second moment of area about the centroidal axis parallel to the base, and about the base itself. About the centroid: I = b h³/12 = 120 × 200³ / 12 = 120 × 8000000 / 12 = 80 × 10⁶ mm⁴. About the base: I = b h³/3 = 120 × 8000000 / 3 = 320 × 10⁶ mm⁴. Turning the beam on its side, so the depth becomes 120 mm, gives I = 200 × 120³ / 12 = 28.8 × 10⁶ mm⁴, less than half as stiff.
chapters.trap: Using the diameter d where the radius r belongs, and mixing units — mm⁴ in one line and m⁴ in the next — which makes answers wrong by powers of ten.
chapters.prereq: 4.1 for the element of area and its distance from an axis; basic integration.
chapters.leave: Shifting I to other axes goes to 4.5; the polar version goes to 4.6; mass moment goes to 4.8.

chapters.idea: A second moment about any axis equals the second moment about the parallel centroidal axis plus the area times the square of the distance between them, and for a thin flat area the two centroidal second moments add up to the polar one.
chapters.depth: Parallel axis theorem I = Ī + A d², with Ī in mm⁴ about the centroidal axis, A in mm², d in mm between the two parallel axes, and I always larger than Ī. Stress that the centroidal axis must be the one in the formula. Perpendicular axis theorem Ix + Iy = J = Iz for a thin flat area in the xy plane, with Iz through the centroid; state that it does not apply to a thick plate or a general solid. Apply both to composite sections built from rectangles: an I-section, a T-section, a channel, an angle, and a rectangle with a hole. Procedure: fix a reference line, find ȳ by the table of 4.2, then add each part's own Ī and its A d².

figure.title: Shift rule for a second moment
figure.aria: A flow shows the second moment about the centroidal axis being shifted by A d squared to a parallel axis and then summed over the parts of a composite section.

chapters.example: Take the T-section with a web 20 mm wide and 80 mm tall and a flange 100 mm wide and 20 mm thick, whose centroid is 67.8 mm above the base. Find the second moment about the horizontal centroidal axis. Web: Ī = 20 × 80³ / 12 = 853333 mm⁴, d = 67.8 − 40 = 27.8 mm, A d² = 1600 × 27.8² = 1236544 mm⁴. Flange: Ī = 100 × 20³ / 12 = 66667 mm⁴, d = 90 − 67.8 = 22.2 mm, A d² = 2000 × 22.2² = 985680 mm⁴. Total I = 853333 + 1236544 + 66667 + 985680 = 3.14 × 10⁶ mm⁴.
chapters.trap: Shifting from a non-centroidal axis, or adding A d² to a moment that already refers to the base; and using the perpendicular axis theorem on a long shaft where it does not hold.
chapters.prereq: 4.2 for locating the composite centroid; 4.4 for the standard values of Ī.
chapters.leave: The polar moment itself goes to 4.6; the product of inertia needs a parallel axis rule of its own in 4.7.

chapters.idea: The polar moment of inertia is the second moment taken about a point rather than a line, and the radius of gyration is the single distance at which the whole area could be concentrated to give the same second moment.
chapters.depth: Define J = ∫ r² dA about the origin, with r the distance to the point in mm and J in mm⁴; show J = Ix + Iy for a flat area, which is the perpendicular axis theorem used in 4.5. Give J = πd⁴/32 for a solid circle and π(D⁴ − d⁴)/32 for a hollow one, and note that J governs the twist of a shaft. Define radius of gyration k = √(I/A) and polar radius k_p = √(J/A), both in mm, so that I = A k². Standard values: rectangle h/√12 about the centroidal axis, circle d/4 about a diameter and d/√8 about the centre. Say that k is the size of the equivalent concentrated ring of area.

figure.title: From polar moment to radius of gyration
figure.aria: A flow builds the polar moment as the integral of r squared dA, splits it into Ix plus Iy, and defines the radius of gyration from it.

chapters.example: A solid steel shaft has diameter 60 mm. Find the polar moment of area about the centre, the second moment about a diameter, and both radii of gyration. A = π × 30² = 2827.4 mm². J = πd⁴/32 = π × 60⁴ / 32 = π × 12960000 / 32 = 1.27 × 10⁶ mm⁴. About a diameter, I = J/2 = 636173 mm⁴, which also equals πd⁴/64. k = √(I/A) = √(636173 / 2827.4) = √225 = 15 mm, that is d/4. k_p = √(J/A) = √(1272345 / 2827.4) = 21.2 mm, that is d/√8.
chapters.trap: Adding Ix and Iy for a point that is not the centroid, and using the diameter in place of the radius when quoting k = d/4.
chapters.prereq: 4.4 for second moments and 4.5 for the perpendicular axis theorem.
chapters.leave: The twist of a real shaft needs the torsion formula from a later strength of materials course; mass radius of gyration goes to 4.8.

chapters.idea: The product of inertia measures how lopsided the area is about a pair of axes, and for every flat area there is a pair of axes, the principal axes, about which it vanishes and the second moments reach their largest and smallest values.
chapters.depth: Define Ixy = ∫ xy dA in mm⁴ with its sign, and note it is zero when either axis is an axis of symmetry or when one of them is a principal axis. Parallel axis rule Ixy = Īxy + A x̄ ȳ, with x̄ and ȳ measured from the centroid of the part to the new origin. Rotation of axes: Ix′ and Ixy′ in terms of Ix, Iy, Ixy and θ. Principal moments I₁,₂ = (Ix + Iy)/2 ± √(((Ix − Iy)/2)² + Ixy²) and the angle from tan 2θp = −2Ixy / (Ix − Iy). Draw Mohr's circle for inertia: centre (Ix + Iy)/2 on the I axis, radius as in the formula, Ixy plotted downwards. Only a few universities teach the full three-dimensional inertia tensor and its eigenvalues; treat that in two lines.

figure.title: Finding the principal axes

nodes.label: I₁ = centre + R, I₂ = centre − R

figure.aria: A flow takes Ix, Iy and Ixy into a Mohr circle whose centre and radius give the two principal moments and the angle of the principal axes.

chapters.example: A right-angled triangle has base b = 60 mm along the x-axis and height h = 90 mm along the y-axis, with the right angle at the origin. Find Ix, Iy, Ixy about the centroidal axes, then the principal moments and their angle. Ix = b h³/36 = 60 × 729000 / 36 = 1215000 mm⁴. Iy = h b³/36 = 90 × 216000 / 36 = 540000 mm⁴. Ixy = −b²h²/72 = −(3600 × 8100)/72 = −405000 mm⁴. Centre = (1215000 + 540000)/2 = 877500 mm⁴. Half difference = 337500 mm⁴. R = √(337500² + 405000²) = 527192 mm⁴. I₁ = 877500 + 527192 = 1.405 × 10⁶ mm⁴ and I₂ = 877500 − 527192 = 0.350 × 10⁶ mm⁴. tan 2θp = −2(−405000)/675000 = 1.2, so 2θp = 50.2° and θp = 25.1° from the x-axis.
chapters.trap: Losing the sign of Ixy, and using the product of inertia about a non-centroidal pair of axes in the principal moment formula without first shifting it.
chapters.prereq: 4.4 for Ix and Iy; 4.5 for the parallel axis shift of a second moment.
chapters.leave: Three-dimensional products of inertia and the inertia tensor are only touched on; the dynamics that uses principal axes comes in Unit 6.

chapters.idea: For a body with mass, the same distance-weighted sum with mass elements in place of area elements gives the mass moment of inertia, which is the resistance of the body to angular acceleration.
chapters.depth: Define I = ∫ r² dm, with dm in kg, r in m and I in kg·m²; mass from density times volume, m = ρV with ρ in kg/m³. Standard results: thin plate of sides a and b about the centroidal axis normal to it, m(a² + b²)/12; plate about an edge, m b²/3; rectangular prism; solid cylinder about its axis, ½ m r², and about a transverse centroidal axis, m(3r² + h²)/12; solid cone about its axis, 3/10 m r²; solid sphere, 2/5 m r²; thin ring, m r². Composite bodies: pick one axis, shift each part with the parallel axis rule I = Ī + m d², add. Link to I = m k². Keep the arithmetic in metres and kilograms.

figure.title: Mass moment of inertia, one rule
figure.aria: A flow builds the mass moment of inertia from the integral of r squared dm and lists the standard values for a plate, a cylinder, a cone and a sphere before combining them.

chapters.example: A solid steel disc has radius 200 mm, thickness 50 mm and density 7850 kg/m³. Find its mass moment of inertia about the central axis and about a diameter. Volume = π × 0.200² × 0.050 = 6.283 × 10⁻³ m³. Mass = 7850 × 6.283 × 10⁻³ = 49.3 kg. About the axis: I = ½ m r² = 0.5 × 49.3 × 0.200² = 0.986 kg·m². About a diameter through the centre: I = m(3r² + h²)/12 = 49.3 × (3 × 0.0400 + 0.0025)/12 = 49.3 × 0.1225 / 12 = 0.503 kg·m². The radius of gyration about the axis is k = √(0.986 / 49.3) = 0.141 m.
chapters.trap: Using millimetres for r while the mass is in kilograms, which gives an answer a million times too large, and shifting with the area A d² of 4.5 instead of the mass m d².
chapters.prereq: 4.5 for the parallel axis idea; 4.6 for the radius of gyration; the density and volume work from first-year physics.
chapters.leave: Using these moments in rotation and general plane motion goes to Unit 6; work-energy and angular momentum methods go to Unit 6 as well.
